title: Social Network Analysis
body: \titlepage
note: Welcome. Build directly on the first class. All small networks are synthetic. The core session is 180 minutes including a 15-minute break. Appendix slides are optional.

title: What we will explain today
note: Explain that students need sums and matrix multiplication, not prior eigenvalue theory. Eigenvectors will be introduced through a repeated calculation.

title: Recall: the adjacency matrix
body:
With rows as senders and columns as receivers,
\[A_{ij}=1\text{ if }i\to j,\qquad A_{ij}=0\text{ otherwise.}\]
\[\mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{out}}=A\ones,\qquad
\mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{in}}=A^{\mathsf T}\ones.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ones$ is a column vector of $n$ ones.
\item In an undirected graph, $A=A^{\mathsf T}$.
\item The order of actors must agree in every matrix and vector.
\end{itemize}
note: Ask what A times a column of ones does. Matrix-vector multiplication is a set of row sums here. Reintroduce transpose explicitly.

title: Our six-person network
body:
\begin{columns}[c]
\column{.54\textwidth}\centering\network{A/B,A/C,B/C,C/D,D/E}
\column{.43\textwidth}\[A=\Atoy\]
\end{columns}\medskip
Node order: A, B, C, D, E, F. Ties are undirected unless stated otherwise.
note: Return to the advice graph from class 1. F is a member with no observed ties. Ask whether C and D play the same role. The graph has six nodes and five edges.

title: Vectors attach values to actors
body:
Let $x_i$ be an attribute of actor $i$, such as an indicator of receiving information.
\[\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item Only A has value 1 initially.
\item $(A\mathbf{x})_i=\sum_j A_{ij}x_j$: add the values of $i$'s neighbours.
\end{itemize}
note: Compute the B row by hand. This sum is not yet a probability or a diffusion model: it aggregates neighbour values. An actual process needs assumptions about timing and transmission.

title: Matrix-vector multiplication: a weighted sum
body:
For three actors, consider
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}.\]
\[M\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}0\times1+1\times2+1\times4\\0\times1+0\times2+1\times4\\0\times1+0\times2+0\times4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}6\\4\\0\end{pmatrix}.\]
Rows of $M$ select the values to sum. The result is another actor-level vector.
note: Use M for this separate three-node directed example to avoid confusing it with the main six-by-six A. M represents A to B, A to C, B to C. Explain dimensions: 3 by 3 times 3 by 1 gives 3 by 1.

title: Direction: receiving values versus sending values
body:
For $A_{ij}=1$ when $i\to j$,
\[(A\mathbf{x})_i=\sum_j A_{ij}x_j
\quad\text{aggregates values of }i\text{'s outgoing neighbours}.\]
If each sender passes its value along every outgoing tie,
\[\mathbf{y}=A^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x},\qquad
 y_j=\sum_i A_{ij}x_i.\]
\textbf{The transpose matters:} collecting neighbour attributes and sending values through ties are different operations.
note: Do not label Ax as forward transmission with row-source adjacency. For an undirected graph the operations coincide. Values are copied along ties in this example; mass is not conserved unless rows are normalised.

title: Exercise: follow the indices
body:
Use the three-actor matrix
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}.\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item Calculate $M^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}$.
\item Which actor receives values from two senders?
\item Why is the result different from $M\mathbf{x}$?
\end{enumerate}
note: Pairs, four minutes. Ask students to write one sum with explicit indices before calculating the whole vector.

title: Answer: values arriving along directed ties
note: Keep the vector values distinct from degrees. This is an algebraic aggregation, not observed information flow.

title: Matrix multiplication links two steps
body:
\[(A^2)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}A_{kj}.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item Choose an intermediate actor $k$.
\medskip\item The product is 1 when both $i\to k$ and $k\to j$ exist.
\medskip\item Sum over all possible intermediaries.
\end{itemize}
Thus $(A^2)_{ij}$ counts \textbf{walks of length two} from $i$ to $j$.
note: Use a binary unweighted graph. Matrix powers with weighted entries sum products of weights, not unweighted walk counts.

title: A worked two-step connection
note: The row is row A, the column is column D. Point to A-C-D on the graph. This same formula is a common-neighbour count in an undirected network.

title: Walks, paths, and matrix powers
body:
\begin{itemize}
\item A \textbf{walk} follows adjacent ties and may repeat actors or edges.
\medskip\item A \textbf{path} does not repeat actors.
\medskip\item $(A^\ell)_{ij}$ counts length-$\ell$ walks, not necessarily paths.
\end{itemize}
\[A\!\to\! B\!\to\! A\quad\text{is a two-step walk, not a path.}\]
In our undirected graph, $(A^2)_{ii}=k_i$: one return walk through each neighbour.
note: Use arrows here to show the order of traversal, not directed edges in the undirected graph. In a directed network diagonal A squared counts reciprocal return walks and need not equal degree.

title: Exercise: two-step counts
body:
\begin{center}\network{A/B,A/C,B/C,C/D,D/E}\end{center}
Without multiplying the whole matrix, find:
\[(A^2)_{AA},\qquad(A^2)_{AB},\qquad(A^2)_{AE}.\]
List the contributing walks. Can a zero entry in $A^2$ rule out a longer connection?
note: Four minutes, individual then compare with a neighbour. Expected 2, 1, 0. A reaches E in three steps.

title: Answer: what a zero does and does not mean
note: For this graph A cubed at A,E is exactly one. Distinguish no tie, no walk of a particular length, and unreachable.

title: Reachability from matrix powers
body:
For distinct actors in a finite graph,
\[j\text{ is reachable from }i
\iff \sum_{\ell=1}^{n-1}(A^\ell)_{ij}>0.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item If any walk exists, a path exists after removing loops in the walk.
\medskip\item A path visits each actor at most once: its length is at most $n-1$.
\medskip\item This explains reachability; software usually uses graph-search algorithms.
\end{itemize}
note: This is a statement for nonnegative binary adjacency, with reachability between distinct actors. Do not recommend computing huge matrix powers for large sparse networks: counts grow and numerical overflow becomes possible.

title: Shortest paths and geodesic distance
body:
\[d(i,j)=\min\{\ell\geq1:(A^\ell)_{ij}>0\}\qquad(i\ne j).\]
\begin{itemize}
\item Set $d(i,i)=0$.
\medskip\item If $j$ is unreachable from $i$, set $d(i,j)=\infty$.
\medskip\item Here $d(A,E)=3$ via A--C--D--E, but $d(A,F)=\infty$.
\end{itemize}
Unweighted distance counts ties. It does not measure physical distance or elapsed time.
note: A shortest unweighted walk between distinct actors is a path: a repeated cycle could be removed to shorten it.

title: The distance matrix
note: Use Delta to avoid confusing distance matrix with degree diagonal D in the appendix. Ask students to read C,E and E,C, then F,A. Infinity is not a missing-data code.

title: Connected components
body:
A component is a maximal set of actors connected by paths.
\begin{center}\network{A/B,A/C,B/C,C/D,D/E}\end{center}
\[\{A,B,C,D,E\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\{F\}.\]
Reordering nodes by component makes $A$ block diagonal: no ties, and no walks, cross between blocks.
note: Maximal means no further node can be added while preserving connection to the set. An isolate is a component of size one. Our node order already groups components, with a five-by-five block and a zero block.

title: Connectivity in a directed graph
note: The graph is a directed acyclic nomination network. F forms its own weak and strong component. Advice-seeker to source arrows are nomination direction, not guaranteed direction of advice transmission.

title: Bridges and articulation points
note: Count all components, including F. Removing C creates AB, DE, and F: three instead of two. Removing D creates ABC, E, and F. E is a leaf, but not an articulation point. Definitions here are for the undirected graph.

title: Exercise: alternative routes
note: Six minutes in pairs, including a quick check with another pair. Ask students to distinguish edge removal from node removal.

title: Answer: redundancy changes social position
note: Debrief for seven minutes, drawing the two routes. This anticipates the fractional counting rule in betweenness. B degree rises from two to three and D from two to three. F remains isolated.

title: Break
body: \begin{center}\Large 15 minutes\end{center}
note: Resume at minute 90. Ask students to keep the original graph handy for the centrality calculations.

title: Centrality depends on the research question
body:
\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Question & Candidate measure\\\midrule
How many direct partners? & Degree\\
How near are reachable others? & Closeness / harmonic\\
Who lies on shortest routes? & Betweenness\\
Who connects to highly scored actors? & Eigenvector / PageRank\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}
\bigskip
No single measure establishes influence, expertise, or power. Tie meaning and assumptions about the social process come first.
note: Frame social position as multiple structural dimensions. A broker, a popular source, and an actor with prestigious contacts may be different people.

title: Degree and its matrix form
body:
\[\mathbf{k}=A\ones,\qquad C_D(i)=\frac{k_i}{n-1}.\]
For the undirected graph:
\[\mathbf{k}=(2,2,3,2,1,0)^{\mathsf T}.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item Normalising divides by the largest possible degree.
\medskip\item C has $C_D(C)=3/5=0.6$.
\medskip\item Degree ignores indirect connections and alternative routes.
\end{itemize}
note: Brief retrieval rather than reteaching class 1. These are binary loopless degree formulas; weights require strength.

title: Closeness on a connected undirected network
body:
\[C_C(i)=\frac{n-1}{\sum_{j\ne i}d(i,j)}.\]
Consider only the connected five-person subgraph A--E:
\[C_C(C)=\frac4{1+1+1+2}=0.8,\qquad
C_C(D)=\frac4{2+2+1+1}=\frac23.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item Higher closeness means smaller average distance to others.
\item The calculation assumes finite distances to every other actor.
\end{itemize}
note: Explicitly n=5 on this slide, not six. Conventional normalised closeness is reciprocal average distance. It may suit a process where short routes are substantively relevant.

title: What happens when actors are unreachable?
body:
Including F gives $d(C,F)=\infty$.
\[\sum_{j\ne C}d(C,j)=\infty.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item The connected-network closeness formula loses its useful ranking.
\medskip\item Dropping unreachable actors changes the population being compared.
\medskip\item Software conventions differ: always state how unreachable pairs are handled.
\end{itemize}
We will use harmonic centrality for the full six-person graph.
note: Under a literal extended-real reciprocal the connected formula gives zero for everyone; some software omits unreachable nodes instead. igraph closeness omits unreachable nodes and returns NaN for isolates, so do not present its output as the all-six formula. Source: https://r.igraph.org/reference/closeness.html.

title: Harmonic centrality handles unreachable actors
body:
\[C_H(i)=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}\frac1{d(i,j)},\qquad\frac1\infty=0.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item Direct neighbour: contribution 1; distance two: contribution $1/2$.
\medskip\item Unreachable actor: contribution 0.
\medskip\item An isolate has score 0; all six actors remain in the denominator.
\end{itemize}
This is a sum of reciprocal distances, not the reciprocal of a sum.
note: Normalised harmonic centrality lies in zero to one for our unweighted simple graphs. With arbitrary weighted distances its range need not be bounded by one. Source: https://r.igraph.org/reference/harmonic_centrality.html.

title: Exercise: compare distance-based positions
body:
Distances to the other five actors are:
\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Actor & \multicolumn{5}{c}{Distances to the others}\\\midrule
C & 1 & 1 & 1 & 2 & $\infty$\\
D & 2 & 2 & 1 & 1 & $\infty$\\
F & $\infty$ & $\infty$ & $\infty$ & $\infty$ & $\infty$\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}
Calculate normalised harmonic centrality for C, D, and F.
\medskip
Which of C and D has better distance-based access?
note: Four minutes. Require the common denominator five. Tie meanings and model of travel still determine whether this structural advantage is relevant.

title: Answer: harmonic centrality
note: Explain that harmonic centrality differs from closeness even in connected graphs: sum of inverses versus inverse sum. Scores should not be numerically interchanged.

title: Betweenness: participation in shortest routes
body:
For an undirected graph,
\[B(i)=\sum_{\substack{s<t\\s,t\ne i}}\frac{\sigma_{st}(i)}{\sigma_{st}}.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $\sigma_{st}$: number of shortest paths between $s$ and $t$.
\item $\sigma_{st}(i)$: how many pass through $i$ as an internal actor.
\item Unreachable pairs contribute 0; endpoints do not count.
\end{itemize}
Betweenness assumes shortest routes are relevant to the process under study.
note: Unordered pairs avoid double counting in an undirected graph. Directed betweenness sums ordered source-target pairs. Brokerage in practice does not necessarily follow shortest paths. Source: https://r.igraph.org/reference/betweenness.html.

title: Counting C's betweenness
body:
\begin{center}\network{A/B,A/C,B/C,C/D,D/E}\end{center}
The pairs whose unique shortest route passes through C are
\[\{A,D\},\quad\{A,E\},\quad\{B,D\},\quad\{B,E\}.\]
Each contributes 1, so $B(C)=4$. Similarly, $B(D)=3$.
\medskip
Pairs involving F are unreachable and add nothing.
note: D lies between A,E; B,E; and C,E. A,B are endpoints for some routes but never internal on a shortest route. Count explicitly rather than equating bridges with scores.

title: Equal shortest paths split the contribution
note: Make clear this separate diamond graph illustrates counting only; node labels differ from the main graph. Avoid reporting U or V total betweenness as one half without including all pairs.

title: Normalising betweenness
body:
There are $\binom{n-1}{2}$ unordered pairs excluding actor $i$.
\[C_B(i)=\frac{B(i)}{\binom{n-1}{2}}
=\frac{2B(i)}{(n-1)(n-2)}.\]
For C in the six-person graph:
\[C_B(C)=\frac4{\binom52}=\frac4{10}=0.4.\]
The denominator includes pairs involving F, even though they contribute zero to the numerator.
note: Use n=6 consistently. Component-only normalisation would give a different score, 4/6 for C in the five-node component. Directed normalisation uses (n-1)(n-2). Source: igraph betweenness documentation.

title: Different measures describe different positions
body:
\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
Actor & Degree & Harmonic & Betweenness & Eigenvector\\\midrule
A & 2 & .567 & 0 & .824\\
B & 2 & .567 & 0 & .824\\
C & 3 & .700 & 4 & 1.000\\
D & 2 & .600 & 3 & .567\\
E & 1 & .433 & 0 & .256\\
F & 0 & .000 & 0 & .000\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}
A and D have equal degree. D has more brokerage; A has more recursive centrality.
\medskip
{\footnotesize Harmonic normalised by $n-1$; betweenness raw; eigenvector scaled to maximum 1.}
note: Values checked in igraph. Explain eigenvector column only intuitively for now: A connects to B and C, both strongly embedded. We derive it after discussing weights. Different columns have different scales; compare actors within columns, not numerical values across columns.

title: Which position matters for your question?
body:
\begin{itemize}
\item Reaching many direct collaborators: consider degree or strength.
\medskip\item Access through short routes: consider harmonic centrality.
\medskip\item Connecting otherwise separated circles: examine brokerage and alternative routes.
\medskip\item Being nominated by highly scored sources: consider recursive prestige measures.
\end{itemize}
What additional evidence would you need before calling an actor ``influential''?
note: Three-minute discussion. Require students to name a tie definition and a plausible process. Prestige as receiving nominations is not identical to contact volume.

title: Weights can mean strength or distance
body:
\begin{itemize}
\item For shortest paths, weights must represent \textbf{costs or lengths}: larger means harder or farther.
\medskip\item Interaction frequency usually represents \textbf{strength}: larger means more frequent contact.
\medskip\item If appropriate, define a separate cost $\ell_{ij}=1/w_{ij}$ for $w_{ij}>0$.
\end{itemize}
\medskip
That conversion is a substantive assumption, not an automatic correction.
In igraph, \texttt{weights = NA} explicitly requests unweighted paths.
note: Distance-based igraph measures use the weight attribute by default when present. PageRank and eigenvector centrality treat positive weights as strengths instead. Never blindly reuse interaction counts as distances. Sources: igraph betweenness, harmonic centrality, and PageRank documentation.

title: Recursive centrality: neighbours' scores matter
body:
Degree assigns every neighbour the same contribution:
\[k_i=\sum_j A_{ij}\times1.\]
Eigenvector centrality instead uses the neighbours' scores:
\[x_i=\frac1\lambda\sum_j A_{ij}x_j.\]
An actor receives a high score by connecting to other highly scored actors.
\medskip
We need scores that are mutually consistent across the whole network.
note: Work with the undirected graph first so the matrix orientation is unambiguous. This is a definition of recursive importance, not independent evidence of influence.

title: An eigenvector keeps its direction under multiplication
body:
Collect the actor scores in $\mathbf{x}$:
\[A\mathbf{x}=\lambda\mathbf{x},\qquad\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{0}.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathbf{x}$ is an \textbf{eigenvector}; $\lambda$ is its \textbf{eigenvalue}.
\medskip\item Multiplication changes the scale of $\mathbf{x}$, not its direction.
\medskip\item For a connected undirected graph with nonnegative ties, use the positive leading eigenvector.
\end{itemize}
Scale is arbitrary: if $\mathbf{x}$ works, so does $c\mathbf{x}$ for $c>0$.
note: Leading means the eigenvalue equal to the spectral radius for a nonnegative adjacency. In our graph the isolate has score zero and the five-node component supplies the leading vector. Do not claim all eigenvectors are centrality scores.

title: Repeated multiplication builds recursive scores
body:
Start with $\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=\ones$ and iterate:
\[\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(t+1)}=A\mathbf{x}^{(t)},\qquad
\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)}=\frac{\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(t+1)}}{\max_i\widetilde{x}^{(t+1)}_i}.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item First update: proportional to degree.
\item Further updates count neighbours weighted by their previous scores.
\item Normalisation prevents the values from growing without bound.
\end{itemize}
Our non-bipartite connected component supports convergence. Other graphs can need different numerical treatment.
note: The triangle makes the nontrivial component non-bipartite. Plain power iteration can oscillate on bipartite graphs; do not demonstrate it as universally convergent. For this graph the initial isolate score becomes zero after one multiplication. Notebook includes a shifted iteration extension.

title: Checking an eigenvector numerically
body:
For our graph, with maximum score set to 1,
\[\mathbf{x}\approx(.824,.824,1,.567,.256,0)^{\mathsf T},
\qquad\lambda\approx2.214.\]
For actor C,
\[(A\mathbf{x})_C=x_A+x_B+x_D
\approx.824+.824+.567=2.215\approx\lambda x_C.\]
For actor E,
\[(A\mathbf{x})_E=x_D\approx.567\approx2.214\times.256.\]
{\footnotesize Small discrepancies reflect rounding.}
note: Show the residual Ax minus lambda x in R. A is symmetric, so ordinary symmetric eigen decomposition applies. A and B have equal values due to their identical surrounding roles under interchange.

title: Directed prestige needs the transpose
body:
With $A_{ij}=1$ for $i\to j$, incoming prestige satisfies
\[x_j\propto\sum_i A_{ij}x_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}=\lambda\mathbf{x}.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item A directed acyclic graph has no positive adjacency eigenvalue.
\medskip\item Disconnected graphs may concentrate scores in one component.
\medskip\item Prestige depends on what a nomination represents.
\end{itemize}
Our directed advice graph is acyclic: PageRank is a more useful recursive example here.
note: For a DAG adjacency is nilpotent: sufficiently high powers are zero. igraph uses the left adjacency eigenvector for directed eigenvector centrality. Do not run directed eigen_centrality on this DAG as if it returned meaningful prestige. Source: https://r.igraph.org/reference/eigen_centrality.html.

title: PageRank: share attention across outgoing ties
body:
Define a row-stochastic matrix $P$:
\[P_{ij}=\frac{A_{ij}}{k_i^{\mathrm{out}}}\quad\text{if }k_i^{\mathrm{out}}>0.\]
\begin{itemize}
\item An actor divides its attention across outgoing neighbours.
\item At a node with no outgoing ties, use a uniform row: $P_{ij}=1/n$.
\item With probability $1-\alpha$, jump to an actor sampled from $\mathbf{v}$.
\end{itemize}
Here $\mathbf{v}=\ones/n$ and $\alpha=0.85$.
note: This is a mathematical random-surfer model following the stated nomination arrows, not a literal account of how advice travels. Uniform dangling rows match the uniform teleportation example used in the notebook. Positive edge weights would normalise by outgoing strength.

title: PageRank as a linear system
body:
For a column vector of probabilities $\mathbf{p}$,
\[\mathbf{p}=\alpha P^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{p}+(1-\alpha)\mathbf{v},
\qquad\sum_i p_i=1.\]
Rearrange:
\[\boxed{(I-\alpha P^{\mathsf T})\mathbf{p}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{v}.}\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $I$ leaves a vector unchanged: $I\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p}$.
\item $0<\alpha<1$ and positive uniform teleportation give a unique probability vector.
\end{itemize}
note: Show that an n-by-n matrix multiplies an n-by-one vector on both sides. Notebook solves this system and compares with igraph. It is not necessary to compute an explicit matrix inverse. Source: https://r.igraph.org/reference/page_rank.html.

title: Linear algebra connects the measures
body:
\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Operation & Network interpretation\\\midrule
$A\ones$, $A^{\mathsf T}\ones$ & Out-degree, in-degree\\
$(A^\ell)_{ij}$ & Number of length-$\ell$ walks\\
First nonzero power at $(i,j)$ & Shortest unweighted distance\\
$A\mathbf{x}=\lambda\mathbf{x}$ & Undirected recursive centrality\\
$(I-\alpha P^{\mathsf T})\mathbf{p}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{v}$ & PageRank\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}\end{center}
Harmonic centrality and betweenness use shortest-path information derived from the graph.
note: One-minute recap. Avoid claiming all measures are simple matrix powers: betweenness also needs counts and participation of shortest routes.

title: R practical: verify, compare, and explain
body:
Open \texttt{code/Lecture2\_SNA.Rmd}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Verify one matrix product and one two-step walk count.
\medskip\item Calculate distances, components, and centrality scores.
\medskip\item Add B--D and explain which actor's position changes.
\medskip\item Verify $A\mathbf{x}\approx\lambda\mathbf{x}$ or the PageRank linear system.
\end{enumerate}
note: 150--153: setup and task allocation. Notebook core tasks are sized for the 25-minute practical; PageRank and advanced extensions can be completed after class. Students with slower setup work in pairs.

title: Key R operations
body:
\begin{lstlisting}
A %*% x                 # Matrix-vector multiplication
A %*% A                 # Two-step walk counts
A^2                     # Elementwise square: a different operation

distances(g, weights = NA)
components(g)
harmonic_centrality(g, normalized = TRUE, weights = NA)
betweenness(g, normalized = FALSE, weights = NA)
eigen_centrality(g, weights = NA)$vector
\end{lstlisting}
For binary $A$, \texttt{A\^{}2} equals $A$ and does not count two-step walks.
note: 153--159: students complete task 1 then compare their distances and scores. Note R uses elementwise powers for matrices; matrix powers must be built with matrix products. Functions were checked against igraph documentation.

title: Perturbation: add one alternative route
note: 159--168: nine-minute perturbation task. C degree remains three; raw betweenness falls four to one. B becomes one, D remains three. Bridge and articulation-point status give a separate view of indispensability.

title: Interpret the results as a researcher
body:
Choose one actor and explain its position using two measures.
\begin{itemize}
\item State the tie definition and the population being analysed.
\medskip\item Explain the measures' different assumptions.
\medskip\item Identify one conclusion the scores do not support.
\end{itemize}
\medskip
Optional mathematical check: compare an eigenvector residual or manual PageRank with the package output.
note: 168--175: pairs write three sentences and discuss two examples as a class. Do not require every pair to finish the PageRank extension within the session.

title: Exit question
note: Three minutes individually. Use answers to assess whether students distinguish direct ties, alternative routes, and repeated actors.

title: What you should take away
body:
\begin{itemize}
\item Matrix products describe indirect routes and neighbour aggregation.
\medskip\item Connectivity determines which actors can reach one another.
\medskip\item Centrality measures capture different structural positions.
\medskip\item A new alternative route can change brokerage without changing degree.
\medskip\item Scores require a tie definition and a plausible social interpretation.
\end{itemize}
note: 178--180: exit answer: the new edge provides an alternative route bypassing the actor; matrix multiplication permits repeated actors, such as A-B-A. Next class: collecting, preparing, and visualising empirical network data.

title: Reading and references
note: Reference slide outside the timed session. All plotted networks and numerical examples are synthetic. The notebook includes reproducible calculations and checks.

title: Appendix: the graph Laplacian
body:
For an undirected graph, let $D=\operatorname{diag}(k_1,\ldots,k_n)$.
\[L=D-A,\qquad L\ones=\mathbf{0}.\]
For actor $i$,
\[(L\mathbf{x})_i=k_ix_i-\sum_j A_{ij}x_j
=\sum_j A_{ij}(x_i-x_j).\]
The result compares the actor's value with its neighbours' values.
\medskip
The number of zero eigenvalues of $L$ equals the number of connected components.
note: Optional extension, not part of the 180 minutes. For the six-node graph there are two zero eigenvalues. Use D for the degree diagonal and Delta for distances. This is for undirected graphs with nonnegative weights.

title: Appendix: a quadratic form measures disagreement
note: Optional. Binary values x=(0,0,0,1,1,0) give energy one because only C-D crosses between values. This connects later to community detection without deriving a clustering algorithm.

title: Appendix: structural equivalence
body:
Actors can have similar positions without being adjacent.
For distinct $i$ and $j$, compare ties to all other actors:
\[A_{ik}=A_{jk}\quad\text{for all }k\notin\{i,j\}.\]
For directed data, compare incoming ties as well.
\medskip
In our undirected network, A and B have identical ties to everyone outside their pair. Interchanging A and B leaves the graph unchanged.
\medskip
\textcolor{accent}{Centrality describes a score; equivalence compares patterns of relations.}
note: Optional sociological extension. The pair-excluded definition accommodates adjacent actors; strict full-row equality would fail due to the diagonal and mutual edge entries. Distinguish structural equivalence from looser role or regular equivalence.

title: Appendix: a stable power iteration
body:
On a connected undirected graph with at least one edge, use
\[\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(t+1)}=(A+I)\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\]
followed by normalisation.
\begin{itemize}
